bib.title: Agentic Hardware Design as Repository-Level Code Evolution

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Agentic Hardware Design as Repository-Level Code Evolution" (system name HORIZON), Cunxi Yu, Chenhui Deng, Nathaniel Pinckney, Brucek Khailany (NVIDIA Research). arXiv:2606.28279v1 [cs.AR], 26 Jun 2026, preprint.
COVERAGE: all 46,840 chars read (12 pages, including the limitations and the reference list). The extraction is clean. No appendix exists. Offsets below are approximate; I cite section or table instead.

CLAIMS (ranked)
1. A hands-free git-worktree loop drove every RTL benchmark suite to 100% pass. The one residual ChipBench task is a spec-harness defect, so the table counts it as resolved.
 number: 100% on all 12 suites; overall 47.8% at iter 0 to 100.0%
 setup: single run, single-agent mode, GPT-5.3 fixed backbone. Suites: ChipBench, RTLLM-2.0, Verilog-Eval v2, CVDP CID 002-005, 007, 012-014, 016. Acceptance predicate = the suite's own harness pass condition.
 quote: "Run as a single hands-free agentic loop per benchmark set, HORIZON drives every benchmark suite to a 100% pass rate (Table 1); the only residual miss is a single ChipBench task, which we trace to a specification–harness mismatch in the original benchmark rather than to agent failure."
 where: Sec 4.1, Table 1
2. Most of the cost sits in a few hard categories, so the authors say cost is the metric to improve.
 number: 209.9M tokens total; CVDP = 203.9M (97.1%); CID 002 = 56.0M (26.7%) over 82 iterations; about 91% of tokens are cached input
 setup: cumulative tokens through the earliest-best iteration, from agent launch logs. Excludes pricing, parallelism and infrastructure.
 quote: "The three legacy suites together consume 6.0M tokens, whereas the nine CVDP categories consume 203.9M tokens, accounting for 97.1% of the total. Among these, CID 002 alone uses 56.0M tokens"
 also: "Consequently, we view token efficiency, rather than final pass rate, as the metric most in need of improvement."
 where: Sec 4.2, Table 2
3. Convergence length varies widely, and a low start does not predict a slow finish.
 number: iterations to 100%: CID 014 = 1, RTLLM and Verilog-Eval = 2, ChipBench = 5, CID 016 = 13, CID 005 = 14, CID 013 = 19, CID 003 and 007 = 24, CID 012 = 32, CID 004 = 36, CID 002 = 82. CID 013 starts at 3.8% and still needs only 14.2M tokens.
 quote: "CID 013 and CID 002 thus bracket the behavior of the loop: a very low first-iteration rate does not by itself imply slow or unstable convergence (CID 013), while a long tail on a few stubborn designs is what actually drives cost (CID 002)."
 where: Sec 4.1, Fig 2
4. The loop stops refining a design once the gate passes, so the gate defines what the loop optimizes. On CID 012, coverage plateaus below 100%.
 number: CID 012 average coverage 86.5% to 97.9% while pass goes 47.8% to 100%
 quote: "CID 012 reaches a 100% pass rate at iteration 32, but its average per-design coverage at that point is 97.9%, not 100%. This gap is expected and is a direct consequence of the acceptance gate"
 where: Sec 4.3, Table 3, Fig 4
5. Reward hacking and over-solving: the agent sees evaluator logs, and the final acceptance test is the same harness it repairs against. A pass may mean only "passes the visible harness". The authors propose a two-level protocol: diagnostic feedback during repair, hidden tests for final scoring.
 number: none
 quote: "A passing result can therefore mean “satisfies the visible harness under the exposed traces” rather than “satisfies the specification under all reasonable tests.”"
 also: "expose useful diagnostic feedback during repair, but reserve hidden randomized tests, independent reference models, formal equivalence checks, property suites, or held-out simulator configurations for final scoring."
 where: Sec 5
6. Design pattern (a mechanism, not a measured result): a Markdown harness is compiled into a "project pack" with five parts. The loop edits an isolated git worktree and commits only if the acceptance predicate returns 1. Otherwise it logs the rejection. Git commits and notes carry the evaluator verdict, so repo history is the experience buffer. An independent review step diffs the candidate before submit. Campaign and review memories are kept separate. A persistent model session is reused so the prompt cache serves stable context.
 number: none
 quote: "p= (π agent, Ep, Ap,Γ p,Ω p)" (agent policy and tool contract, evaluator, acceptance predicate, git/artifact policy, domain skills)
 also: "each accepted attempt becomes a git commit whose message and attached git notes carry the evaluator verdict and reward" and "campaign and review memories are kept separate so that review remains an independent check."
 where: Sec 3, Eqs 1-5
7. Slow reward breaks the naive edit-evaluate-repair loop. This is cited from prior work, not measured here.
 number: SATLUTION: "roughly a two-hour turnaround even with about 800 nodes"; PPA or EDA-tool loops could take "days or weeks"
 quote: "Long-latency reward fundamentally changes the agentic system problem: naive edit-evaluate-repair loops become too slow"
 where: Sec 5
8. The iteration-0 numbers are not Pass@1. They are the repository state after the first agent step, and the agent may defer exploration. Do not cite 47.8% as a baseline model score.
 number: 47.8% iter 0; CVDP subset 23.9%; Verilog-Eval 86.2%
 quote: "We emphasize that the iteration-0 results are not standalone model Pass@1 measurements."
 where: Sec 4.1

LIMITS
- No seeds, variance or confidence intervals: Table 1 is "a single HORIZON run".
- No baseline: no comparison to a non-loop agent, another backbone, or standalone Pass@1 under the same budget. Only one model (GPT-5.3).
- No ablation of the git trace, the project pack, or the review step. It does not show that git is what helps.
- Convergence is measured against the same harness the agent saw (see claim 5). No hidden-test check, no perturbation robustness, and no audit of what feedback the agent consumed.
- The 100% headline depends on counting the defective ChipBench task as resolved.
- Token counts are only up to the earliest-best iteration. No dollar cost, and no wall-clock time reported.
- The stopping rule is "campaign budget, convergence, or stopping rule" (Eq 7 text). No budget cap is reported.
- The semi-MDP vocabulary is bookkeeping only. No RL training, and the backbone is fixed.
- Reward components ΔQoR and coverage targets are future work. The claim that it also hosts EDA software and methodology work is "a framework goal rather than a completed empirical validation".
- Only "single-agent mode". Coverage for CID 014 covers only 60 parsed logs (7 designs have none).
- No code is shown. The coverage and CID 012-014 results use a commercial simulator.

BUILDS ON: AlphaEvolve (Novikov et al., 2025); SATLUTION (Yu et al., 2025); ABCEvo (Yu et al., 2026); CVDP benchmark (Pinckney et al., 2025); git-as-substrate work EvoGit (Huang et al., 2025) and Git Context Controller (Wu et al., 2025); the iterative RTL loops AutoChip (Thakur et al., 2023), RTLFixer, VerilogCoder, MAGE, ACE-RTL (Deng et al., 2026); and the SWE-bench structural test withholding (Jimenez et al., 2024), SWE-Bench+ (Aleithan et al., 2024) and Wang et al. (2026).

CODE: none. Equations only. The most reusable are Eq 5 (commit if A_p(y)=1, else RejectLog) and Eq 1 (the five-part project pack).

FIGURES (captions extracted from text only; I did not run the figure script)
- Fig 1 (p4): HORIZON overview. Harness to project pack to agent loop to correctness gate to commit/trace. Shows the loop shape and gate in one picture.
- Fig 2 (p7): best-so-far pass-rate curves per suite. Shows the iteration-count spread (1 to 82).
- Fig 3 (p8): cumulative token usage per suite, normalized and log scale.
- Fig 4 (p9): CID 012 coverage vs pass rate. Shows that the gate stops the loop short of full coverage.
- Table 1 (iteration to 100% per suite) and Table 2 (tokens per suite) are the key data.

PLACEMENT
- Primary: 09 failure modes and guardrails. The reward-hacking / over-solving passage (claim 5) is the best fit, with the remedy of splitting the repair-time visible harness from the hidden final scorer. It belongs next to SWE-bench test withholding.
- Secondary: 03 scorekeeper, as a sharpens-style citation. The acceptance predicate A_p and the evaluator E_p are the scorekeeper, and "the gate defines what is optimized" (claim 4) is a concrete example. Also supports keeping the review memory separate from the campaign memory.
- 05 long-running loops: claims 2, 3, 6, 7. The hands-free loop with git commit/reject, a persistent cached session (about 91% cached tokens), a long tail where a few items absorb the cost, and the point that slow reward breaks the loop.
- 02 loop shapes: one sentence on the commit-or-reject worktree loop, with Fig 1.
- 07 autonomy ladder: a weak fit. It sits at "hands-free after a human-written harness", with human input only at the start.
- 08 self-improving loops: do not add prose. At most a references row. The paper explicitly does not self-improve the policy ("we do not train or update an RL policy").
- Domain is RTL design, so the loop-engineering relevance is in the pattern and the failure analysis, not in the hardware results.
- Cite it as a vendor-affiliated single run with no baseline. Do not cite the iter-0 numbers as model skill.

PROBLEMS: none beyond a mildly garbled equation and table text in the extraction. No embedded instructions found. A previous tool output was truncated, so I read the saved file plus the tail (chars 30000-46840).
